Synthesis of allenynes via Pd-catalyzed coupling
of 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonates with boronic acids †
Jie Wang,
 a Hui Qian
 *a and Shengming Ma
 *a,b
Conjugated allenynes widely exist in natural products and are commonly employed in the development of
functional materials. However, synthetic methods are very limited. In this contribution, a palladium-cata-
lyzed cross-coupling reaction of 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonates with a series of commercially available boronic
acids using S-phos or Gorlos-phos as the ligand has been developed. Diversely substituted allenynes
incorporating synthetically useful functional groups are obtained in good yields under this set of mild
conditions. Gram-scale reactions and synthetic transformations have been conducted to show their
potential utility.
Introduction
Allenynes are typical units existing in some biologically active
natural products, 1 such as marasin 2 and mycomycin, 3 with
high antibiotic activity. In addition, conjugated allenynes are
not only key structures in various functional materials 4 but
also unique reactive intermediates in organic synthesis. 5
However, approaches towards allenynes are still limited.
Palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions of terminal
alkynes or alkynyl organometallic reagents with propargylic
derivatives or allenic halides have been developed
(Scheme 1a).
6 Recently, our group realized the EATA
(enantioselective allenation of terminal alkyne) reaction to
aﬀord various conjugated chiral allenynes with excellent
enantioselectivity and regioselectivity: a catalytic reaction of
copper halides with mixed oxidation states in the presence of
commercially available ( S)- or ( R)-α,α-diphenylprolinol
(Scheme 1b).
7 Here, we wish to report a new general method
for the synthesis of conjugated allenynes: Pd-catalyzed cross-
coupling reaction of 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonates with commer-
cially available boronic acids using S-phos or Gorlos-phos as
the ligand under mild conditions, which may tolerate various
synthetically useful functional groups (Scheme 1c).
Results and discussion
Initially, the ligand e ﬀect of the coupling reaction was investi-
gated (Table 1). We chose 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonate 1a and 1.1
equiv. of (3-methoxyphenyl)boronic acid 2a as the model sub-
strates using Pd 2(dba)3·CHCl3 as the catalyst in 1,4-dioxane at
room temperature in the presence of H 2O (2 equiv.) for
12 hours. Among the typical monophosphine ligands, PCy 3
aﬀorded the desired allenyne 3aa in 59% NMR yield with 19%
recovery of 1a (entry 1). When PPh 3 was employed, no expected
product 3aa was formed with 91% recovery of 1a (entry 2).
When tri(tolyl)phosphines were employed, tri( o-methylphenyl)
phosphine could furnish the corresponding product 3aa in
Scheme 1 Approaches towards conjugated allenynes catalyzed by
transition metals.

83% yield (entry 3); tri( p-methylphenyl)phosphine did not
perform well (entry 4). Relatively electron-deficient monopho-
sphine, o-(diphenylphosphino)benzaldehyde, led to 90% recov-
ery of 1a (entry 5). Then we found that X-phos could also
deliver 3aa in 74% yield with 14% recovery (entry 6); a high
yield of 87% was achieved with no recovery when S-phos was
used (entry 7). LB-phos,
8 Gorlos-phos,9 and Zheda-phos 10
developed by our group were also tested (entries 8 –10) and
Gorlos-phos was found to be compatible with this cross-coup-
ling reaction in a yield of 74%. Common bisphosphine ligands
BINAP, DPPF, DPPB, and BIPHEP failed to give the allenyne
product 3aa.
We next screened various palladium catalysts and solvent
with S-phos as the ligand (Table 2). The reaction led to 88%
recovery of 1a when Pd
2(dba)3·CHCl3 was replaced with
Pd(PPh3)4 (entry 2). The yield of the product was improved to
89% yield when Pd(dba) 2 was employed (entry 3), but
Pd(dmdba)2 aﬀorded product 3aa with lower e ﬃciency
(entry 4). Among the Pd( II) catalyst, only Pd(OAc) 2 could aﬀord
allenyne product 3aa in a poor yield (entries 5 –7).
With Pd(dba) 2 as the catalyst, the solvent e ﬀect was next
investigated. The reaction was inhibited when DCM was used
as solvent (entry 8). To our delight, THF and toluene could
aﬀord allenyne 3aa in almost quantitative yields (entries 9 and
12). The yield decreased to 65% or 36% when reducing the
loading of the catalyst or removing H 2O. Therefore, the
optimal reaction conditions were defined as 4 mol% Pd(dba) 2,
8 mol% S-phos, and 2 equiv. of H 2O in THF at room
temperature.
Having established the optimal conditions, the generality
of this Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling reaction was examined
(Scheme 2). First of all, a series of commercially available aryl-
boronic acids were reacted with 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonate 1a.
Besides phenylboronic acid, the aryl group may also be substi-
tuted with electron-donating groups, such as methyl, meth-
oxyl, or phenyl at the p-position, smoothly forming allenynes
3ab–3ad and 3af in moderate to high yields. The steric e ﬀect is
not obvious since o-, m- and p-methoxy-substituted phenyl
boronic acids all a ﬀorded 3ae, 3aa, and 3ad in >80% yields.
Synthetically useful p-fluoro, p-chloro and p-bromo-substituted
phenylboronic acids could all a ﬀord the corresponding pro-
ducts 3ag–3ai in decent yields of 63 –87%. Electron-deficient
p-trifluoromethyl ( 3aj), m-nitro ( 3ak), p-cyano ( 3al), p-formyl
(3am), and p-acetyl ( 3an) may all be tolerated. In addition,
2-naphthyl, 3-thienyl, and 3-furanyl-substituted boronic acids
all worked to a ﬀord allenynes 3ao–3aq in decent yields.
Furthermore, cyclopentenyl boronic acid may also be applied
aﬀording product 3ar in 44% yield. With phenylboronic acid,
R

and halo-, cyano-, silylether-substituted alkyl groups forming

allenynes 3bb–3gb in 63 –93% yields. R 1 may also be phenyl,
aﬀording 3hs in 56% yield. Gorlos-phos was also tested in
1 mmol reactions, a ﬀording the desired products 3aa, 3ad–3af,
and 3an in 67 –88% yields. To further expand the scope of
allenyne, non-symmetric 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonate 1i was
employed under the standard conditions. The reaction pro-
ceeded smoothly, however, the regioselectivity was not satisfac-
tory with the formation of 3ia and 3ia′ in a 1 : 1.2 ratio.
Three di ﬀerent reactions on a gram-scale were conducted
under the standard conditions to a ﬀord the target products
3aa, 3ae, and 3gb in 79 –92% yields (Scheme 3). The synthetic
potential of compound 3gb has been demonstrated: the pro-
tecting group TBS could be easily removed with camphorsulfo-
nic acid a ﬀording diol 4 in 88% yield
11 and the subsequent
esterification formed ester 5; stereoselective iodohydroxylation
of 3gb with NIS and H 2O could deliver the useful intermediate
2-iodoallyl alcohol 6 in 76% yield ( Z/E = 20 : 1).12
A catalytic cycle has been proposed as shown in Scheme 4.
LnPd(0) coordinated with the S-phos or Gorlos-phos ligand
would undergo S N2′-type oxidative addition with 1,4-diyn-3-yl
carbonate 1 to generate the allenylpalladium intermediate I

(1.1 mmol), Pd(dba) 2 (4 mol%), S-phos (8 mol%), and H 2O (2 equiv.) in
THF (5.0 mL) at room temperature unless otherwise noted. a 1a
(1.0 mmol), 2 (1.1 mmol), Pd 2(dba)3·CHCl3 (3 mol%), Gorlos-phos
(12 mol%), K 2CO3 (12 mol%), and H 2O (2 equiv.) in dioxane (5.0 mL) at

after releasing a molecule of CO 2. Then the methoxy anion
would be protonated with water to form allenylpalladium
hydroxide intermediate II,13 which would more e ﬃciently
undergo transmetalation with boronic acid 2 to generate inter-
mediate III. Finally, the desired product allenyne 3 would be
aﬀorded after reductive elimination with the regeneration of
the catalytically active species L nPd(0).
Conclusions
In summary, we have developed a Pd-catalyzed cross-coupling
reaction of 1,4-diyn-3-yl carbonates with a series of commer-
cially available boronic acids with S-phos or Gorlos-phos as the
ligand. Under this set of mild reaction conditions, a variety of
allenynes with synthetically useful functional groups are
obtained in good yields. Three gram-scale reactions and the
synthetic potential of the products have been demonstrated.
Further studies on this topic are currently underway in our
laboratory.
Conﬂicts of interest
There are no conflicts to declare.
